To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the liver injury in acute hepatitis B is due to the immune response to HBs antigen, which is not completely suppressed even after the fourth week of the disease, and that the immune responses to HBs antigen are not affected by pregnancy.

in pregnant women, the disease is mild and recovery is early, but in adult men and non‐pregnancy women, the disease continues beyond the fourth week and the recovery is late, even though the HBsAg persists in the serum for a long time.
the evolution of immune responses to HBV in acute hepatitis B is associated with the severity of liver cell damage and the persistence of HBsAg.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the pathogenesis of acute hepatitis B in the Indian population.
the mechanisms of liver cell injury in acute hepatitis B in relation to the immune response to HBV.
the mechanisms of liver cell damage and the immune responses in acute hepatitis B in adult male and female patients and in pregnant patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the liver cell necrosis in acute hepatitis B is due to a complex interplay of HBV replication, the immune response to HBV, and host factors.
the evolution of the immune response is different in acute hepatitis B in pregnancy and in adult male and in non‐pregnant females.

in adult male and female patients with acute HBV infection, liver cell damage continues for a longer period than is clinically apparent, and that this is probably associated with a vigorous T cell response to HBs antigen.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the immune response to HBs Ag is the major determinant of liver cell damage and that the immune response is more vigorous in males and non‐pregnancy females than in pregnant women.
in acute hepatitis B the liver cell necrosis, as indicated by elevated ALT levels. is associated with HBsAg in the serum and the presence of T‐cell response to HBsAq.
, in adult male patients and non‐pregnantly pregnant female patients, HBV infection leads to liver cell injury which is followed by an immune response to viral antigens.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of large amounts of HBsAg in the serum, even after the patient has recovered clinically, may not necessarily indicate the presence of active viral replication.
the presence of HBsAg in serum in high amounts is not associated with clinical recovery.
, in acute hepatitis B in adults, the immune response to the virus is not fully evolved by the seventh week.
